chapter: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
title: Duke arranged Cootie's departure to Goodman
summary: When Goodman approached him Cootie told Duke, who set up the deal and later told him he was too big to come back.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: How did that happen? How -- you'd think that Duke felt, well, if he was going to go out on his own, well, then he was going to, and so he wished him well?
Yeah. Duke was very nice about that. Things like that. You know. He did the same thing with me.
Yeah. Tell me about what he did with you. How he did it.

Well, the first time I was contacted by Goodman, I told him about it. I told Duke about it. And we used to go out and talk, talk about it, so he would tell me what to tell him the next time he called. And he set up the deal for me.
(Laughter)

And we used to go out at night. And he said, 'Well, go ahead on. You've got a chance to make some money. And make a name for yourself.' And I left. And I said, 'Well, I'll be back in a year, after the contract is over with.' After the contract was up, I contacted him and I said, 'I'm ready for my job. The year's up.' He said, 'Oh, no, you're too big now. You can make a whole lot of money.' He said, 'Go ahead on.' He said, 'I don't need you right now.' 'Time I need you, I'll let you know.'
How about that. That's really -- I mean
there's few bandleaders would let guys who are the main guys in their band, just see them bow out, or help them to bow out, are there?

Yeah. But -- but he was nice in things like that. He did the same thing for Johnny, as you said. He gave him Billy Strayhorn, to go along with him and help him along. And after Johnny's thing was over, Johnny came on back and Billy Strayhorn came on back. They had a deal together there.
Well, did he put any money in it?
Uh-uh. They didn't need any money in it.
Oh.
He didn't need to put any money in it.

Well, it's really extraordinary that anybody would do that. It's really amazing. I mean, you don't -- in the business world, you would never find a guy at the head of a firm, and take one or two of his main men and say, 'Yeah, with my blessing, you go and start your own firm.' You know?
But I don't think -- it didn't hurt him. It wouldn't hurt him.
Well, it hurt him to lose you, Cootie, --
No.
-- and it hurt him to lose Johnny -- yes,
well, you know it did.
I don't think so.
Why do you say that?
I just don't think so, it hurt him.
It didn't hurt him at all to lose me.
Well, Cootie --
Or Johnny.
Well, Cootie, in this sense it didn't, I mean, that he was certainly big enough, and he was talented enough to be able to fix it so that the loss didn't show.
Yes.

Or didn't flag him. But -- but you know, I mean, the fact is that -- I don't suppose -- I mean, we talk about people being at their peak. You talk about Louis being at his peak with Les Hite. Well, I don't suppose the Ellington band was ever so perfect as when Cootie and Johnny were in that band, before they ever left. I think that must have been -- that was a peak. There's no question of that. Everything has its time, doesn't it?
Yeah.
I guess it --
But, in a situation like that, it didn't hurt to.
No. Well, I didn't mean, you know --
No.
I didn't mean that you were harming him.
He was glad.
No. No, it didn't.
It didn't hurt him at all.
And probably one of the things, too, is that he was always so adventurous, that the challenge of producing something different there --
Yeah.
-- to have it come up different.
Yeah.
But he didn't -- you know, that was a challenge to him, that he enjoyed coping with that challenge, didn't he?
And I thought the band sounded very, very good. Without me and Johnny Hodges.
(Laughter)
Well, listen --
I thought the band sounded wonderful.
